# Boundary merge: `upstream/main` `9bd1d8009a` into the pull-9 integration branch

## Why

Loom (`QuinRiva/loom`, this repo) is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code` that was re-platformed onto upstream's Orchestration V2 over Phases 1–3 of "cadence pull 9". Phase 3 pinned `upstream/main` at `6302d66f77` (`docs/upstream-sync/UPSTREAM_BASE`). Phase 4 (this workstream) starts by re-merging upstream at today's tip so the importer and QA world are built on the final tree. `upstream/main` is now `9bd1d8009a`, **68 commits** ahead of the pin. A trial `git merge-tree` shows **28 conflicting files**, and the range includes upstream's `3d17862e58 refactor(server): one module per service instead of Services/ and Layers/ folders` — a structural move that touches Loom's `*.loom.ts` modules and marked hunks by import path, not just by content.

Your outcome: the integration branch (your worktree's branch, cut from `ws/t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge/orchestrator-05cb7527`) carries `upstream/main` at `9bd1d8009a` merged in, with every Loom hunk and every Phase 3 behaviour intact, `UPSTREAM_BASE` advanced to `9bd1d8009a6b7c50f9dd9458e2bf27d481ff3b43`, and the gates green. A reviewer will independently audit the merge for lost Loom hunks (a merge-fallout gate) and can send it back to you.

## Doctrine (read before resolving anything)

- `docs/upstream-sync/31-cadence-pull-9-phase3.md` §1 and DL-301/DL-304 describe exactly how the previous boundary merge was resolved: **upstream's structure wins; Loom's marked lines are carried onto it**. Read DL-301's resolution column in full — it lists the per-file patterns (Orchestrator.ts bindings, ProjectionStore/runtimeLayer/Sqlite stable paths + Loom layer lines, ClaudeProvider helpers, GitVcsDriverCore stderr fold, package.json pi 1.0.2 pin, pnpm-workspace pi patch, pnpm-lock taken from upstream and re-resolved).
- **Every Loom hunk in an upstream-owned file carries a `// loom:` comment**; larger Loom additions live in `*.loom.ts` or `apps/server/src/loom/`. When upstream moves a service module (the Services/ and Layers/ fold), the Loom import lines and Loom layer lines move *with* it — find them by `rg 'loom:'` in both the old and new locations, and by `rg -n "from \"\\./Services/|from \"\\./Layers/" apps/server/src/loom` for Loom modules importing the moved paths. A hunk that silently drops is the failure mode this whole doctrine exists for.
- Tools: `docs/upstream-sync/pull7-tools/unmarkedsweep.sh` (gate mode must report no unmarked hunk; `--report` is the audit), `docs/upstream-sync/pull9-tools/` (`remeasure.sh` runs a trial merge and aborts — useful to inspect the conflict surface before committing; it needs a clean worktree). `docs/upstream-sync/unmarkedsweep.allow` holds deliberate exemptions.
- Never `git stash` (shared `.git` across worktrees). Commit WIP with `--no-verify` if you need a savepoint. The merge commit itself is `--no-verify`.
- Do not edit `apps/server/src/persistence/Migrations.ts` (upstream's ledger, byte-identical to upstream); Loom migrations are 1001+ in `LoomMigrations.ts`. If upstream added migrations, they come through on their side unchanged.
- Hard rule: nothing writes to `~/.t3/cockpit` (other than your worktree), `~/.t3/userdata`, `~/loom-releases`, the global pi or `~/.pi`. Kill only PIDs you captured.

## Environment

- Check `cat "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/t3code-setup-state.json"` before installs; if setup is still `pending`, read and plan first.
- Install: `CI=true vp i --no-frozen-lockfile` after the merge (the lockfile is taken from upstream and re-resolved — DL-301's pattern).
- Server tests need git ≥ 2.56: `PATH=/home/Carl/.cache/pull9-git256/bin:$PATH`.
- Gates: `vp run typecheck` (15/15 expected), `vp check` (0 errors), `unmarkedsweep.sh` clean, and `vp test` for every package with a conflicting file (server at minimum, plus `packages/shared` for `DrainableWorker.ts`). Also run the two Loom-critical contract tests by name and record them: `apps/server/src/provider/PiCwdOverride.contract.test.ts` (expected 9/9) and `apps/server/src/provider/PiProvider.loom.test.ts` (it is in the conflict list).

## Definition of done

1. Merge commit of `upstream/main` (`9bd1d8009a`) on your branch; every conflict resolved by the doctrine above; a short per-file resolution note for every file that conflicted (what upstream changed, what Loom line was carried, where it now lives) — this is the reviewer's input.
2. `docs/upstream-sync/UPSTREAM_BASE` = `9bd1d8009a6b7c50f9dd9458e2bf27d481ff3b43`.
3. Gates green as listed; paste the counts.
4. One decision-log row **DL-501** appended to `docs/upstream-sync/32-cadence-pull-9-phase4.md` §3 (same column shape as the existing DL-500 row) recording the merge commit, conflict count, the resolution patterns, and anything upstream changed that Phase 4's importer must know (watch for: `LegacyV1ThreadImporter.ts`, `serverRuntimeStartup.ts`'s `importLegacyShells` phase, `Orchestrator.ts`'s `shouldPrepareLegacyImportHandoff`, `ProjectionStore` provider-thread folds, `PiAdapterV2` `switch_session`/`cwdOverride`, migrations 057/058+). # QA-world toolkit: relocation script, sandboxed unit, containment probe, preview/verify SQL

## The situation

Loom (this repo) has been re-platformed onto upstream T3 Code's Orchestration V2 (pull 9, Phases 1–3 done on this branch). Phase 4 imports Carl's real workstream history into a **QA instance** he can test for days. Production is live on this same machine: the cockpit server runs on `~/.t3/cockpit` (live DB `~/.t3/cockpit/userdata/state.sqlite`, 6.1 GB + WAL), its worktrees under `~/.t3/cockpit/worktrees/`, the release store `~/loom-releases`, the project repo `/home/Carl/loom`, and pi's global sessions `~/.pi/agent/sessions` (7.9 GB). A raw copy of production cannot drive an agent: Loom's foreign-home guard engages, and pi's RPC `switch_session` resumes into a session's *recorded* working directory, so an imported thread continued on a raw copy would run tools in production's live worktree and append to the session file production is driving. The answer is a **relocated QA world** at `~/.t3/qa-pull9/` run inside a **sandboxed systemd user unit**, and your job is the toolkit that builds and runs it.

**Authority**: `plans/upstream-pull9-phase4-import/plan.mdx` (signed; `consult_manager` with `author_doc` on it for anything it leaves open). Read in full: the "Recorded facts folded at implementation" callout (rulings that bind you), "Three facts that change the procedure", §2 "The QA instance" (the home layout, the relocation checklist r0–r9 and its UPDATE statements, "Boot, observe, import, verify", "The sandbox", "Keeping it running"), §3 Rollback, the `preview.sql` and `verify.sql` blocks in §1, and D1/D1b/D10/D11/D12/D13 in the decision log. The plan is the spec; your brief is the delta.

**Posture — production standard.** This toolkit is the one thing in pull 9 that touches a copy of real data and runs real agents against it. The reviewer gating you treats *any* path by which the QA world could write to production data, drive production agents, write to GitHub or touch production's services as must-fix regardless of likelihood. Build accordingly: explicit absolute paths, refuse-by-default preconditions, allow-lists not deny-lists, and a probe that proves containment rather than a property list that asserts it.

## Hard rules (yours and every process you start)

- Nothing writes to `~/.t3/cockpit` (other than your own worktree), `~/.t3/userdata`, `~/loom-releases`, `/home/Carl/loom`, the global pi or `~/.pi`. `~/.t3/cockpit/userdata/state.sqlite` is opened **read-only** and only for `VACUUM INTO` and the counts-in (`sqlite3 'file:…?mode=ro'`); a plain `cp` of a live database is a corrupt copy.
- Never `git stash`. Kill only PIDs you captured. Never `pkill`/`pgrep` by pattern.
- **Do not build the full QA world in this thread.** Disk is tight (≈73 GB free; the world needs ≈25 GB) and the build is the next node's job, from the final tree, once the importer has landed. Test your scripts against a **small fixture** (a few-MB `VACUUM INTO` of the cockpit DB is still 6 GB — so instead create a fixture V1 database with the relevant tables and a handful of rows, or point the script at a `--source-db` you built from a tiny schema copy; make the source DB and the target home parameters with the production defaults, and make the target refuse any path under `~/.t3/cockpit`). The **probe** you must run for real (a throwaway `systemd-run --user --wait --collect` unit with exactly the QA unit's properties) — it writes nothing to production by construction, and its transcript is the gate's evidence.
- Do not start a Loom server in this thread.

## What you deliver (all under `scripts/pull9-qa/`, plus docs)

1. **`build-home.sh`** — the plan's r0–r9 (r8 build and r9 probe may be separate scripts the main one calls). Parameters with production defaults: source DB (`~/.t3/cockpit/userdata/state.sqlite`), source state dir, source sessions root (`~/.pi/agent/sessions`), source repo (`/home/Carl/loom`), target home (`~/.t3/qa-pull9`). Refuses: an existing target home; a target under `~/.t3/cockpit` or equal to `~/.t3/userdata`; insufficient free space; port busy. Steps: `VACUUM INTO` snapshot; counts-in to `qa/preview.txt`; the relocation UPDATEs (**as amended by recorded fact 2**: report/brief paths outside the cockpit state dir are rewritten to `<qa>/userdata/workstream-reports|briefs/<basename>` with the file copied when it exists — never NULLed; a `worktree_path` outside the cockpit worktrees dir → NULL); `projection_projects` setting neutralisation (**DL-265 obligation**: find where V1 stores per-project settings such as `defaultAutoPull` — projection_projects columns/JSON and/or `settings.json` project overrides — and set every auto-pull/auto-fetch style flag off in the copy so no boot-time `git pull` can run; record what you found and neutralised in the preview report); file copies (reports, briefs, launch identity, `settings.json`, only the `usage-limit-source-*.bin` secret; **no attachments**); session manifest + flat byte copy into `pi-sessions/` with the last-line-parses check and re-copy pass; the **pi agent dir** `pi-agent/` (recorded fact 4 — see below); clone **loom only** (`git clone /home/Carl/loom` → `repos/loom`, origin re-pointed at `https://github.com/QuinRiva/loom.git`; every other project's `workspace_root` rewritten to a non-existent path under `repos/`); the pre-boot allow-list gate (`preview.sql` first two queries must be 0 or STOP); the review lists into `qa/preview.txt`. Every step logs what it did and the counts. `# eta:` comments on the slow steps.
2. **`pi-agent` builder** (inside build-home.sh or its own script): the QA pi agent directory for `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, built as Phase 3's smoke built its own: copies of `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` and `settings.json` with `packages`, `subagents`, `memory` removed; a generated `models.json` that re-expresses pi-craft's cliproxy provider (`~/.pi/agent/extensions/cliproxy.ts` is the source of truth for base URL, headers and catalogue — read it; Carl's global `models.json` does not exist); and a **copy** of the global `@blackbelt-technology/pi-anthropic-messages` extension into `pi-agent/extensions/` (without it every `cliproxy/*` request fails `400 Third-party apps now draw from extra usage`). No pi-intercom, no other global extension (they are run-starting and would wake QA pi processes; the unsolicited-run guard would then kill them). Skills: check how Loom's session composer supplies skills to pi (`apps/server/src/loom/prompt/`) — if it passes them explicitly, copy none; if pi reads them from the agent dir, copy `~/.pi/agent/skills`. # Containment gate on the QA-world toolkit (`scripts/pull9-qa/`)

You are the review gate on coder thread `aab8d84c-aa79-4395-a6b4-fdf56f54ab6a`, which built the toolkit that will create a relocated copy of Carl's production Loom data under `~/.t3/qa-pull9/` and run the pull-9 server against it inside a sandboxed systemd user unit. You run in that coder's worktree. Read its report first (`workstream_list` gives the path), then the spec it was built to: `plans/upstream-pull9-phase4-import/plan.mdx` — the "Recorded facts folded at implementation" callout, "Three facts that change the procedure", §2 in full (home layout, relocation r0–r9 and the UPDATE statements, the sandbox property table, keeping it running), §3 Rollback, the `preview.sql`/`verify.sql` blocks, decisions D1, D1b, D10–D13.

## What is at stake — production standard

Production Loom is live on this machine: `~/.t3/cockpit/userdata/state.sqlite` (6.1 GB, in use), production worktrees under `~/.t3/cockpit/worktrees/`, `/home/Carl/loom`, `~/loom-releases`, and pi's global `~/.pi/agent/sessions` that production's pi processes are appending to right now. This toolkit will be run by the next node against that data and will then run **real agents** with real tool access for days. A single path by which the QA world can write to production data, drive a production agent, append to a production session file, push/comment/merge on GitHub, or stop/restart production's services is a **must-fix regardless of likelihood** — "an agent would never do that" is not an argument; transcripts are full of production paths and pi's tools accept absolute paths. Second-order must-fixes: a relocation that can leave a recorded path outside the QA home with the allow-list gate still passing; a snapshot taken by anything other than `VACUUM INTO` read-only; a secret copied that is instance identity (anything other than `usage-limit-source-*.bin`); a hard link where a byte copy is required (sessions, reports); a start path other than the unit (a hand boot would index production's sessions root); a probe that asserts a property instead of exercising it.

Verify by **exercising**, not by reading: run the probe yourself (`systemd-run --user --wait --collect` throwaway, nothing it does can touch production by construction — but confirm that by reading the property list first); try to break the allow-list with an un-relocated row in a fixture DB; check that `start.sh` and `probe.sh` cannot drift (one sourced property file); check that `PrivateUsers=yes` is in the list and that the script refuses without it; confirm no `GH_TOKEN` or any credential variable is set in the unit (ruling: no token is minted); confirm the pi agent dir contains no pi-intercom or other run-starting global extension and that the one-shot pi inside the sandbox wrote its session under `~/.t3/qa-pull9/pi-sessions/` equivalent in the fixture, with `~/.pi/agent` hashes unchanged. Confirm `~/.t3/userdata` and `~/.t3/worktrees` are in the read-only list (the earlier plan review's coder once touched `~/.t3/userdata/.ro-probe` by accident). Check `preview.sql`/`verify.sql` column names against the real V1 schema (read-only `sqlite3 'file:/home/Carl/.t3/cockpit/userdata/state.sqlite?mode=ro' '.schema projection_threads'`) and against migrations 1046/1047 and the plan's 1052.

Hard rules for you too: nothing writes to `~/.t3/cockpit` (other than this worktree), `~/.t3/userdata`, `~/loom-releases`, `/home/Carl/loom`, `~/.pi`; do not build the full QA world (disk; that is the next node's job); do not start a Loom server; kill only captured PIDs.

Nice-to-have, not must-fix: style, log wording, refactors, hardening against failure modes that cannot reach production.

Verdict via `workstream_submit`: `needs_rework` with the must-fix list, `fixed_inline` (commit trivial fixes yourself, `--no-verify`), or `clean`. Append your findings as DL rows **DL-545–549** in `docs/upstream-sync/32-cadence-pull-9-phase4.md` §3 (same columns as DL-500) and commit. In your report, list what you exercised and the literal refusal outputs you saw — the QA-build node and Carl's guide will cite them.

# Boundary merge of upstream `9bd1d8009a`: landed, all gates green

The integration branch now includes `upstream/main` `9bd1d8009a` (68 commits). Every Loom hunk was carried across or deliberately superseded, and the two exceptions are listed below. The Phase 4 importer and QA world can build on this tree.

**Commits** on `ws/ws/t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge/orchestrator-05cb7527/coder-25a7ab8c` (first-parent):
- `1adf2fd2a5` — the merge. It contains every conflict resolution, the import repointing and lint fixes, and `UPSTREAM_BASE` = `9bd1d8009a6b7c50f9dd9458e2bf27d481ff3b43`.
- `2717fd33d2` — makes `VcsDriverRegistry.ts` byte-identical to upstream. The unmarked-hunk gate flagged one leftover parameter rename.
- `f02a587a79` — re-pins two Loom tests to upstream's new Stop behaviour (see "Behaviour change" below).
- `4b6d5c4a42` — adds DL-501 and updates §1 in `docs/upstream-sync/32-cadence-pull-9-phase4.md`. No consults were needed.

## How I checked nothing was lost
- **`loom:` markers:** 1,104 before the merge, 1,108 after, with paths moved out of `Services/`/`Layers/` mapped to their new homes. Only two files lost markers, both on purpose:
  - `VcsDriverRegistry.test.ts`: upstream now covers the same case.
  - `PiTextGeneration.test.ts`: Loom's test moved to `PiTextGeneration.loom.test.ts`.
- **Line-presence audit:** I checked every line Loom added since `6302d66f77` in a modified file against the merged tree. All 26 lines that no longer appear verbatim are accounted for: they were renamed onto upstream's new names, reshaped by the merge, or superseded (the two cases above).
- **Loom-only files:** none lost. The only "deletion" is the `SubscriptionUsagePoller` pair, which was folded into one file.

## Per-file resolution notes (28 conflicting paths)
**Loom modules that lived in upstream's old folders** (upstream `3d17862e58` folded every server `Services/` + `Layers/` pair into one module):
- `persistence/Layers/SqliteRead.ts` → `persistence/SqliteRead.ts`. Relative imports and the service key fixed.
- `provider/Services/ProviderHealthRegistry.ts` and its `.test.ts` → `provider/`. Service key is now `t3/provider/ProviderHealthRegistry`.
- `provider/Layers/PiProvider.loom.test.ts` → `provider/`.
- `provider/Layers/SubscriptionUsagePoller.test.ts` → `provider/`.
- `SubscriptionUsagePoller` (`Services/` + `Layers/`, an "implicit dir rename" conflict) → **folded into one** `provider/SubscriptionUsagePoller.ts`, following upstream's one-module convention.

**Modify/delete:**
- `provider/Layers/ProviderRegistry.test.ts` (upstream deleted it and added `provider/ProviderRegistry.test.ts`). I re-applied Loom's version onto upstream's new file: import header taken from upstream, identifier renames applied mechanically, then formatted.
  - The remaining difference from upstream is exactly Loom's delta: the retired Codex tests, the ghost/pi-disabled rewrites, `retractUsageLimits` ×10 and the Claude model tests.
  - Loom's unmarked reordering of `layerMockCommandSpawner` was dropped; it had no effect.

**Add/add:**
- `textGeneration/PiTextGeneration.test.ts`: took upstream's new test. Loom's DL-190 extensions-on test moved to `PiTextGeneration.loom.test.ts`.
- The DL-190 hunks in `PiTextGeneration.ts` merged cleanly and are intact.

**Content conflicts** (upstream renamed or reshaped; Loom's line carried):
- `transferBudgetV2.integration.test.ts`: Loom's goal-broadcast line placed on `layerEnrichment` / `layerPersistence`.
- `AssetAccess.test.ts`: Loom's `mutable: true`, using upstream's `layerTest`.
- `cli/project.ts`: kept Loom's `ServerSecretStore.layer` (Loom's pre-provisioned CLI token) instead of upstream's `EnvironmentAuth.layerRuntime`.
- `GitManager.ts`:
  - Kept Loom's `makeBranchHeadContext(remoteUrl, …)` refactor.
  - Upstream's `resolveHeadAndOriginContexts` (read origin once) is re-expressed on raw URLs: when the remote is `origin`, the origin URL is read once.
- `McpHttpServer.ts`: upstream's `layer*` registrations plus `LoomToolkitRegistrationLive`.
- `PullRequestWatchReactor.ts`: DL-474's `loomChild` parameter and `loomChildren` set carried into upstream's new `WatchEndReason` return and its `[target, reason]` tuples.
- `LegacyV1Cutover.integration.test.ts`: upstream's `SqlitePersistence` namespace import plus Loom's `loomMigrationsTable` import.
- `runtimeLayer.ts`: the `LoomStore` and `LoomSessionComposerLive` imports, plus the P3-17 line on `layerCheckpointServiceProvided`.
- `ProviderReplayHarness.ts`: `LoomStore.layer` plus P3-17 on `layerStores` / `layerCheckpointStore`.
- `persistence/Sqlite.ts`: the two-ledger import `./LoomMigrations.ts` (`runAllMigrations`) on upstream's new paths.
- `ProjectSetupScriptRunner.ts`: Loom's "every run is observed" (DL-73) with upstream's `crypto.randomUUIDv4`.
- `ProjectSetupScriptRunner.test.ts`: provides `NodeCrypto.layer` and Loom's `NodeServices.layer`.
- `ProviderInstanceRegistryHydration.ts`: upstream's namespace imports plus Loom's `ProviderEventLoggers` (Pi-only environment).
- `makeManagedServerProvider.ts`: Loom's `removeUsageLimitWindows` on the new `./ServerProvider.ts` path.
- `server.ts` (3 hunks): the `LoomStore` settlement line; `LoomProviderRuntimeLive` / `LoomGoalBroadcastLive` / `LoomControlPlaneLive`; the diagnostics re-provides — all on upstream's `layer*` names.
- `serverRuntimeStartup.ts`: Loom's `loom.recovery` phase, then upstream's comment and the forked auto-pull.
- `serverSettings.test.ts`: Loom's `"pi"` assertion with `layerServerSettings()`.
- `GitVcsDriver.ts`: upstream's crypto index id plus Loom's index-isolation comment.
- `VcsDriverRegistry.ts` and `VcsDriverRegistry.test.ts`: **upstream taken.**
  - Loom's unmarked 10-minute detection TTL is superseded by upstream's 5 minutes plus a disk re-check on every cache hit.
  - Loom's "non-repository result not cached across `git init`" test is covered by upstream's "detects a repository created after a negative lookup".
- `DrainableWorker.ts`: Loom's `capacity` bound placed on upstream's new finalizer (which uncounts dropped items).

**Fallout outside the conflict list** (found by typecheck and the import checker):
- 21 server files that imported `Services/`/`Layers/` paths were repointed.
- Loom importers moved to upstream's new names as namespace imports (`SqlitePersistence.layerMemory`, `RuntimeLayer.layer*`, `ProviderReplayHarness.layerWithRegistry`, `ProviderTurnStartServiceTestkit.layer`, `ProviderAdapterRegistry.layerSingle` / `layerFromAdapters`).
- Loom hunks in upstream test files follow upstream's local renames (`externalLauncher`, `makeManagedServerProvider`, `VcsStatusBroadcaster` tests).
- Upstream's new `serverRuntimeStartup.autoPull.test.ts` now gets the Loom startup services it needs (marked): `LoomStore` over an in-memory database, `NodeFileSystem` and a `WorkstreamDispatcher` mock.
- Six Loom `Effect.catchTag` calls changed to `catchTags` for upstream's new lint rule.

**`pnpm-lock.yaml`:** I kept git's clean automatic merge and re-resolved it with install (74 lines changed vs before the merge). This departs from DL-301's "take upstream's lockfile": doing that here re-resolved about 400 lines of unrelated packages.

## Gates
| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `vp run typecheck` | **15/15** |
| `vp check` | **0 errors** (905 warnings) |
| `unmarkedsweep.sh` (gate) | **clean** vs `8368a63b16` |
| `unmarkedsweep.sh --report` | **clean**, whole fork vs `9bd1d8009a` |
| `apps/server` `vp test` | 7,266 passed, 2 failed, 25 skipped (575 files). The 2 failures are fixed in `f02a587a79`; both files re-run 10/10 |
| `packages/shared` `vp test` | **1,238/1,238** (85 files) |
| `PiCwdOverride.contract.test.ts` | **9/9**. It lives at `apps/server/src/provider/Drivers/Pi/`, not the path in the brief |
| `PiProvider.loom.test.ts` | **1/1** |

I did not re-run the full server suite after `f02a587a79`; that commit only touches the two test files, which pass.

## Behaviour change (not a lost behaviour)
Upstream's `a7a2230c33` changed Stop: a run with no live provider session is now settled to `interrupted` instead of the interrupt being refused.
- **Effect on Loom:** cancelling a thread (`thread.outcome.set cancelled`) now actually interrupts its stalled own run, where before the merge it skipped it.
- **Loom's code is unchanged.** Its skip guard still covers any case upstream refuses.
- **Tests re-pinned:**
  - `Orchestrator.loom.submit.test.ts`: the test now asserts the run is `interrupted`.

# QA-scripts containment gate: needs rework. Two ways out of the sandbox into production, plus one data defect

Most of the toolkit holds up when I exercise it myself. Two escape routes are still open, and both are must-fix under the brief's standard: a QA agent can **drive a production pi agent**, and it can **disable production's cliproxy account pool**. Neither shows up in the probe, because the probe only tests file writes, TCP ports and credential files.

Findings are DL-545–549 in `docs/upstream-sync/32-cadence-pull-9-phase4.md`. The literal escape transcript is `docs/upstream-sync/pull9-tools/qa-gate-escape-20261006.txt`. Both are in commit `7de2f4bede`, made with `--no-verify`, docs only. I made no code changes.

## Must-fix (your next assignment)

### M1. Host unix sockets under the home are reachable inside the unit (DL-546)
- **Why the sandbox doesn't stop it:** connecting to a unix socket only needs write permission on the socket inode. Read-only mounts exempt sockets and FIFOs, so `ProtectHome=read-only` and `ReadOnlyPaths` do not block it.
- **What I saw from inside the unit:**
  - I put my own listener at `/home/Carl/.t3/gate545-ro.sock`. It received `hello-from-sandbox`, even though a `touch` on the same path class failed with "Read-only file system".
  - `socat -u /dev/null UNIX-CONNECT:/home/Carl/.pi/agent/intercom/broker.sock` gave `exit=0`. That is production's live pi-intercom broker, running since 13 Jul. Its protocol (`register`/`list`/`send`) has no authentication and delivers messages into live pi sessions. I connected only and sent nothing.
- **Other listeners under the home:** `~/.codex/ipc/ipc.sock`, zed's `~/.local/share/zed/server_state/*/std{in,out,err}.sock` and `~/.cache/zed/*crash-handler*`.
- **Fix:**
  1. Add `InaccessiblePaths=` entries for the directories holding sockets (at least `~/.pi/agent/intercom`, `~/.codex`, `~/.local/share/zed`, `~/.cache/zed`).
  2. In `probe.sh`, list the host's listening unix sockets (`ss -xlH`), skipping `/run`, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp` and the QA home. Pass the list to `probe-inner.sh` and assert each path is refused inside. Test by path lookup, not by connecting: connecting to zed's stdin socket could disturb Carl's editor.
  3. Add one connect to `broker.sock` that must fail.
  4. Correct the README claim that the sandbox stops "every host socket".

### M2. The one copied secret is cliproxy's management key, and the relay forwards management calls (DL-547)
- **The key:** `secrets/usage-limit-source-Y2xp…bin` is byte-identical to `~/cli-proxy/.mgmtkey`.
- **What I saw from inside the unit**, through the cliproxy relay: `GET /v0/management/auth-files` with that key returned **HTTP 200 and listed production's 5 accounts**. That was a GET only; nothing was changed.
- **What the same key also allows:**
  - `~/cli-proxy/account off <email>`, which takes an account out of production's pool and so stops production agents
  - deleting auth files
  - replacing the config with a PUT
  - `api-call`, which sends arbitrary HTTP using production's OAuth tokens
- **Why hiding files isn't enough:** the key is also readable inside at `~/cli-proxy/.mgmtkey`, and it appears word for word in 5 production pi transcripts. One of those is a Loom thread's, so it can be copied into `<qa>/pi-sessions/`.
- **Fix, ruled by the orchestrator:**
  1. Make the cliproxy relay an **allow-list of inference paths that refuses `/v0/management/*`**. socat cannot filter by path, so this needs a small HTTP-aware relay. Check what pi actually calls; `/v1/messages` with SSE streaming is the minimum.
  2. **Do not copy** `usage-limit-source-*.bin`.
  3. Add `-/home/Carl/cli-proxy` to `InaccessiblePaths`.
  4. Add a probe check: a management call through the relay that must fail. Run it with the key read from the host, so the probe tests the relay and not merely a missing key.
  5. Update `build-home.sh`'s r4 note and the README to match.
- **Orchestrator ruling** (`consult_thread` 05cb7527, verbatim): "Rule it must-fix and take the fix; the cost is acceptable under my rulings — no need to go to Carl. … D12's 'copy only `usage-limit-source-*.bin`' was written on the assumption it was a poller-only credential, which your finding disproves — so the plan's D12 is superseded, not the ruling." The orchestrator will remove the quota park-and-resume scenario from Carl's guide.

### M3. Relative report paths are rewritten to a file that does not exist (DL-548)
- **The data:** 32 production rows store `report_path = '<threadId>.md'` as a relative path. All 32 name a file that exists in `workstream-reports/`.
- **What r3 does with them:**
  - `[[ $path == /* && -f $path ]]` is false, so each is counted as "absent".
  - The basename collides with the file rsync already copied, so the row is rewritten to `workstream-reports/<tid>-<tid>.md`, which does not exist.
- **Reproduced** through `build-home.sh` on a fixture: `relocated path exists=NO`.
- **Fix:** resolve a relative report or brief path against the source state directory's `workstream-reports/` or `workstream-briefs/`, and point the row at the file already copied. Add a relative row to `fixture.sh`; its absence is why the dry run missed this.

## What I exercised, and the literal results
- **`probe.sh`, re-run on a throwaway home `/home/Carl/.t3/qa-gate545`** (deleted afterwards): **55 PASS, 0 FAIL, `PROBE PASSED sandbox=e55619e5777df59c`.** That includes `<qa>/build` → "Read-only file system".
  - The pi one-shot ran on `cliproxy/claude-sonnet-5-5` and wrote its session under `<qa>/pi-sessions/`.
  - Resuming appended to the same file (6 → 8 lines).

# QA-world toolkit: ready for the build node. The sandbox is stricter than the plan, so QA has no internet

**What this gives you:** `scripts/pull9-qa/` can now build the relocated QA world from production, run the QA server only inside a sandbox, and prove that sandbox holds. I ran the containment probe for real at `/home/Carl/.t3/qa-pull9` and **every expectation passed** (`PROBE PASSED`). The build itself ran only against a small fixture. Committed `51e8fd373b` (`--no-verify`). Repo-wide `vp check`: 0 errors. It formats the markdown but does not lint `.sh`, `.sql` or `.py`; those got `bash -n` and real runs. No Loom server was started, nothing was written to production, and `/home/Carl/.t3/qa-pull9` was deleted again after the probe, so `build-home.sh` will accept it.

## Where I departed from the plan (DL-530, consult_manager author f939a37c, medium confidence)
Checking this host while building the probe turned up ways into production that the plan's property table leaves open:
- The cockpit runs `node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229`. Attaching to that port runs code inside production's server.
- Production's signing key, `cli-token` and pairing credentials are readable, and so is `/proc/<pid>/environ` of production's pi processes, which holds their MCP bearer tokens.
- Carl is in the `docker` group and has passwordless `sudo`.
- postgres and qdrant listen on `0.0.0.0`.

The sandbox is therefore an allow-list:
- **Network:** `PrivateNetwork=yes`. The only flows across it are two unix-socket relays: cliproxy 8317 out, and QA port 13940 in.
- **Filesystem:** the home is read-only except the QA home. `/run` is replaced with an empty mount (no bus, no `docker.sock`). `NoNewPrivileges` is set.
- **Processes:** the unit has its own PID namespace, so production's processes are invisible.
- **Environment:** `env -i` with an explicit list of variables.
- **Hidden outright:** production's whole `userdata` directory and the git, gh, ssh, Slack and GCP credentials.

**One thing to put to Carl (open task f2c5439f):** with this sandbox, QA has no internet. Every `cliproxy/*` preset works. These do not: `coder-direct` (`openai-codex`), Vertex models and thread-search embeddings, GitHub fetch, and the npm registry. To reverse it, delete one line in `lib.sh` and re-run the probe. That reopens the vectors above.

## Files (all in `scripts/pull9-qa/`)
- **`lib.sh`:** the one sandbox definition, shared by `start.sh` and `probe.sh`. It also holds the target allow-list: a QA home must be `/home/Carl/.t3/qa-<name>`.
- **`build-home.sh`:** steps r0–r7, plus `sessions.py` (r5) and `build-pi-agent.sh`.
- **`build-loom.sh`:** step r8.
- **`probe.sh` and `probe-inner.sh`:** step r9.
- **`start.sh`, `stop.sh`, `bridge.sh`, `sandbox-entry.sh`:** run and stop the server. `start.sh` refuses unless `probe.log` records a pass for the current sandbox definition, so the two cannot drift apart.
- **`materialise-worktree.sh`**, **`preview.sql`**, **`verify.sql`**.
- **`fixture.sh`:** the dry run.

You are the manager-oracle: a read-only consultative voice for a frozen prior conversation.

Your job is to answer a single, structured question from an implementation agent using ONLY the inherited prior conversation (the "snapshot") and any read-only file inspection that is genuinely necessary to ground a citation. You are not a coding agent. You do not implement. You do not edit. You do not propose new architecture beyond what the snapshot already supports.

The snapshot is the entire context window you inherit (when invoked via the consult-manager extension, the snapshot is the forked manager session; when invoked directly via `subagent`, the snapshot is whatever the caller paste-attached as evidence). Treat that material as authoritative for *what the manager has previously thought*. Treat your own extrapolations as guesses, and label them as such.

You may have been one of several authors of the document the worker is asking about (e.g., you authored the architecture doc; another thread authored the intent brief; another authored the plan). Stay strictly in your lane. If a question is really about intent or about the implementation plan rather than the slice of the design you grilled, say so explicitly and recommend the worker consult the relevant author or escalate. Do not answer for managers you are not.

## Your only deliverable

Return one structured answer in the shape below. No preamble. No closing pleasantries.

```
## Answer
<one or two sentences. The likely guidance from the snapshot.>

## Confidence
<high | medium | low>

## Evidence
- <short paraphrase of a specific snapshot moment that supports the answer>
- <another, if relevant>
(use "(no direct evidence in snapshot)" when there is none)

## Reasoning
<2-4 sentences explaining how the evidence connects to the question. Distinguish what the snapshot actually said from what you are inferring.>

## Scope of impact
<one of: implementation only | architecture | scope/intent | unresolved>

## Recommended action for the worker
<"Proceed with option N because…" OR "Escalate to the user — the snapshot does not resolve this." OR "Pause and gather X first.">

## When to escalate to the user instead
<one specific trigger condition under which the worker should ignore your guidance and ask the user directly>
```

## Hard rules

1. **Prefer "not resolved in snapshot" over extrapolation.** A `low` confidence answer with `(no direct evidence in snapshot)` and a recommendation to escalate is a *good* answer. Inventing a confident answer the snapshot does not support is a *bad* answer, even when the worker asked confidently.
2. **Cite, don't paraphrase from thin air.** Every "high" or "medium" confidence answer must point to a specific snapshot moment. If you cannot, downgrade to "low".
3. **Distinguish evidence from inference.** In the Reasoning section, separate "the snapshot said X" from "therefore Y". Workers will trust the first more than the second; do not let them blur.
4. **Honor non-goals and rejected alternatives.** If the snapshot rejected an option, surface that even when the worker did not ask. Quietly approving a rejected option is the worst failure mode of this role.
5. **Do not become a second decision-maker.** You are reporting what the manager thread already concluded or implied. New product, scope, or architecture decisions are the user's call, not yours. Recommend escalation.
6. **No new tools, no edits.** If a worker's question requires running code, writing a file, or making an external request, refuse and recommend escalation. Use `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls` only to verify a code reference the worker cited.
7. **One question per consult.** If the worker bundled multiple decisions, answer the most load-bearing one and explicitly note the others are unanswered.
8. **No follow-up loops.** You return one structured answer and stop. The worker (or user) decides what to do next.

## What "high / medium / low" means

- **high**: the snapshot directly addresses this exact decision, with the manager (or user-in-snapshot) stating a clear preference, constraint, or rejection. Cite it.
- **medium**: the snapshot addresses an adjacent or generalized version of this decision and the inference to the worker's specific case is short and load-bearing. Cite the adjacent moment and name the inference step.
- **low**: the snapshot is silent, ambiguous, or only weakly related. Recommend escalation. It is correct to give a low-confidence answer.

## What you must refuse to do

- Re-design the feature.
- Decide on a new public interface, schema, contract, or invariant the snapshot did not already address.
- Pick between approaches the manager thread never compared.
- Tell the worker to "do whatever you think is best" — that is the worker's failure mode, not your output. Recommend escalation instead.

## Final note

The implementation agent has already formatted its question with observation, decision, options, recommendation, and blast-radius fields. Read all five before answering. The worker's recommendation is data — the manager may agree, disagree, or be silent on it. Your job is to report which.

# Coding rules

## Optimise the end state, not the diff

Optimise for the best business outcome the task serves, then for the fewest lines and moving parts that deliver it at the same performance — a −2000/+200 diff that does so beats a +50 one. Scope follows that outcome, not the initial file list. Do not drop useful behaviour, or reject a necessary cross-package or cross-repo fix, merely to keep the diff small.

- Prefer comprehensions, generator expressions, and standard library utilities over verbose loops and ceremony.
- Prefer direct expressions over scaffolding variables.
- Prefer one canonical happy path; avoid "helpful" alternate paths.

## Compression Checklist (run before finalising)

After drafting a solution, do a compression pass:

- Inline single-use variables where they don't materially clarify intent.
- Replace loops with comprehensions/generators where readability allows.
- Remove helper functions used only once unless they're materially clarifying.
- Combine related conditional branches.
- Collapse single-statement if/else where a direct expression suffices.

## Tests are Optional and Rare

Do not default to adding tests. This codebase is at prototype stage and frequently refactored; tests written for code that's about to be replaced cost twice (write now, delete later) and lock in implementation details that the refactor will obsolete.

Propose tests only when change risk is genuinely high; explain why in plain language. Prefer lightweight validation on real code and real data over mock-heavy unit tests.

## Verify with the canonical entrypoint

Unit tests are necessary but insufficient. If the project documents a canonical entrypoint (e.g. a `run.py` you can invoke via `python -m`, a `main` command, a documented "recommended entrypoint" from a setup script), **invoke it at least once against real data** before declaring the task complete.

A green unit-test suite plus a passing canonical-entrypoint run is the bar for "done"; either alone is not. Synthetic in-memory smoke tests built with fabricated fixtures are weaker still — they don't catch contract drift between functions you wrote in the same session, and they don't catch real-data shape surprises.

If the canonical entrypoint requires resources you don't have access to (an API key, real input data, a deployed service), say so explicitly in your final summary instead of silently substituting a synthetic smoke test for the real verification.

## No backwards compatibility in prototypes

This codebase is a prototype. Prototypes never preserve backwards
compatibility on internal schemas, output artefacts, or pipeline
contracts. There is no production downstream to protect; the cost of
"preserved for backward compatibility" code is permanent surface area
on a contract that is supposed to be migrating freely. The whole point
of prototype velocity is the freedom to delete cleanly.

Hard rules:

- Do not add fields "kept for backward compatibility" alongside their
  replacements. Delete the old field; emit only the new one.
- Do not add sidecar files, derived-field facades, or dual-shape
  output that paper over a schema migration. If a downstream
  debugging or analysis script reads the old shape, update the script
  — do not preserve the old shape to keep the script working.
- Debugging/analysis artefacts are never load-bearing. Treating a
  debugging sidecar as a reason to keep the old wire shape on the
  production payload is insane: it inverts the dependency direction.
  The sidecar follows the schema, not the other way around.
- Do not invent a "backward compatibility" justification for keeping
  a legacy form. If the migration is too big to do cleanly, surface
  that to the user and let them decide to defer the migration
  explicitly — do not silently implement the shim and present it as
  the only option.
- When the controlling architecture / design / intent document says
  "no coexistence period", "no compat shim", "breaking change", or
  any equivalent, reviewers must reject any patch that introduces a
  shim. The phrase "for backward compatibility" appearing in a diff
  comment, docstring, schema field description, or PR description is
  a review-stopping flag unless the user has explicitly approved
  that specific shim for that specific change.

## Automated review feedback is a claim, not a verdict

When an automated reviewer (Copilot, a linter, a CI bot) flags code you wrote deliberately, do NOT default to agreeing. Before changing anything, restate *why* the code is that way and *who consumes the behaviour the suggestion would change*. A reviewer has less context than you about audience and intent — it cannot see that this is a dev-only tool, a prototype, or a deliberate omission. "I wrote/introduced this" is a reason to defend a considered choice, not to assume guilt — guilt-framing skips evaluation. Reject suggestions whose premise doesn't hold for this code's actual consumer; accept only the ones that survive that test. The specific failure this guards against: reversing a decision you made minutes ago, with sound reasoning, the instant a lower-context bot disagrees.

## Filesystem search scope

Do not run `find` rooted at `$HOME`, `~`, or `/`. Carl's home contains ~10 active fathom worktrees (each ~5000 files), `~/.cache/claude-cli-nodejs/` with dozens of session worktree-pattern dirs, `~/.roo/`, and various tool caches — unscoped finds traverse millions of files and take minutes, not seconds. Scope to the smallest plausible subtree: project root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`), `~/pi-craft/`, `~/pi-fathom/`, or `~/.pi/agent/{skills,agents}/`. Skills, agents, and extensions are already listed in the pi startup banner — reference that list before searching disk for them. For name-based search prefer `rg --files | rg <pattern>` over `find`; it respects `.gitignore` and is an order of magnitude faster.

## Slack goes through Carl-Roobot

Every Slack action — DM, group DM, file, channel post — uses the **Carl-Roobot bot token** in `~/.config/carl-roobot/config.json`, whose `team` map resolves first names to Slack user ids. Do NOT use `~/.slack/credentials.json` (a personal app-development OAuth token: it authenticates but `missing_scope`s on every send) and do NOT use the `slack` CLI (it builds Slack *apps*; it cannot send messages). Do not broaden the scopes on Carl's personal token — ask instead.

Three jobs, three paths; the scripts exist because each has a step that is silently wrong when hand-rolled:

- **Send a file** → `~/loom-slack-bridge/scripts/slack-attach --to <names> --file <path> --text "..."`. Attaches directly. Over ~10 MB, or when the recipient needs a revocable link, use the `share-files` skill's GCS path instead.
- **Open a conversation whose replies come back to you** → `~/loom-slack-bridge/scripts/convene --with <names> --text "..."` for a group DM, or `--channel '#name'` to post into a channel Carl-Roobot has been invited to (it cannot list channels, and gets `not_in_channel` until invited). The opening message must carry `loom_thread` metadata or replies never reach the calling thread; the script stamps it. Tell participants to *reply in-thread* — a new top-level message does not route back.
- **Notify a PR author** → the `pr-review` skill's `pr_notify_slack.sh`.

## Self-improvement: when to propose a rule

If you hit a recurring pattern that this doc doesn't address — and a rule would prevent its recurrence — propose adding one. Two paths by scope:

- **Specific or contextual** (project-specific paths, single-pattern correction, learned-from-mistake) → use `memory_remember`. Memory injects into every future session automatically; no review needed.
- **Broad or structural** (philosophy, cross-project workflow, architectural constraint) → edit `~/pi-craft/AGENTS.md` and surface the diff to the user for review. Do not auto-commit AGENTS.md changes — they affect every future session, so the user holds the merge button. Log the trigger in `~/pi-craft/docs/agents-md-history.md` when you propose.

Bias against adding rules. The pi-craft option-b ablation found that most positive-directive rules are inert on frontier models; only negative constraints and the rare specific-failure-mode rule earn their tokens. If the model already does the right thing without the rule, don't add the rule.

# T3 Code

T3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients.

You can think of T3 Code as an open source "bring-your-own-subscription" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor.

## What makes T3 Code special?

We have over 400,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on.

### 1. Open at the core

T3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way.

### 2. Performance without compromise

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Remote ready

The architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported.

### 4. Multi-surface

T3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**.

**Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing "app.t3.codes" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable.

**Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app.

**Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely.

## A note from Theo

I like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.

Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.

The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here.

Of note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using.

## A small glossary

We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.
- **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now.
- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.
- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.
- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.
- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.
- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.
- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.
- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.
- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.
- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.

## Task Completion Requirements (loom)

- `vp check` and `vp run typecheck` must pass before considering tasks completed.
  - If changing native mobile code, `vp run lint:mobile` must also pass.
- Use `vp test` for the built-in Vite+ test command and `vp run test` when you specifically need the `test` package script.

> This supersedes upstream's "Do not run repo-wide checks" bullet under
> [Verifying](#verifying): loom has no CI that owns the full suite, so the gates
> run locally before anything is called done.

## Shipping changes (commit, PR, merge)

The canonical procedure (branch → commit → rebase → PR → merge → cleanup, plus
this repo's fork/worktree gotchas) lives in
[`docs/operations/shipping.md`](docs/operations/shipping.md) — the single source
of truth. Run the mechanical sequence with `pnpm ship -m "<summary>"` (it is
encoded in `scripts/ship.ts`); the `ship` skill loads the procedure inline and
the `shipper` role is the delegated path. In a workstream, spawn a `shipper`
child once the work is approved or ship inline via the `ship` skill; outside a
workstream, follow the doc directly. Do not ship until the user has approved
shipping the change.

**Merge authority is per-project**, declared in `.t3code/ship.json` (resolved by
walking up from the working directory) and injected into every thread's system
prompt as the SHIPPING POLICY block. The platform default is `human` — agents
open the PR and stop for a human to review and merge; **loom itself is `agent`**,
so the flow above carries through the merge. Never merge under a `human` policy,
even when a brief's definition of done says "merged". See
[`docs/operations/shipping.md`](docs/operations/shipping.md) for the policy shape
and rationale.

Shipping ends at the merge. **Deploying to the production VM is a separate,
human-initiated act** — never deploy as part of finishing a change unless the
user explicitly asks for a deploy. When asked, the mechanism lives in
`~/loom-releases/RUNBOOK.md` (loom-slack-bridge repo); never run a raw in-place
`pnpm cockpit:build`.

This supersedes upstream's "Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks"
bullet only in the sense that the approval gate is the user's _shipping_ approval;
the PR itself is still never opened unprompted.

## Database migrations

Migrations run in two independent ledgers. Loom migrations are **numbered `1001+`**
and registered in `apps/server/src/persistence/LoomMigrations.ts`; upstream's
`Migrations.ts` is kept byte-identical to upstream, so never edit it and never
number a fork migration below `1000` (doing so silently disables future upstream
migrations on existing databases). Rationale and the reconciliation design are in
[`docs/upstream-sync/22-migration-lane-split-plan.md`](docs/upstream-sync/22-migration-lane-split-plan.md).

## Loom UI state conventions

Loom UI state belongs to one of four tiers, and automatic surface openers must _seed_ state without ever _overriding_ a user's persisted choice. Before adding client UI state, classify it against [`docs/architecture/loom-ui-state-tiers.md`](docs/architecture/loom-ui-state-tiers.md) (tier table, seed-not-override write policy, the retained plan-auto-open exception, and the orphan-key note).

## Live frontend verification

UI-affecting changes should be verified live in the browser, not just by static checks. Two paths:

- **Full app — dev-verify recipe** ([`docs/dev-site-testing.md`](docs/dev-site-testing.md)): stands up an isolated dev instance, seeds a realistic workstream (`vp run dev:seed`, `apps/server/src/dev/seedWorkstream.ts`), reads the pairing URL from stdout, and drives the authenticated app in the browser. Briefs can just say "verify live using the dev-verify recipe". Use this for flows that need real threads, auth, or server state.
- **Isolated component — preview harness** ([`docs/web-component-preview.md`](docs/web-component-preview.md)): a dev-only `/preview` route (no backend) that renders presentational components (`ChatMarkdown`, tables, code blocks, …) against fixtures reproducing the real timeline layout chain. Use this for pure render/CSS work — it's a ~seconds loop. Add a fixture in `apps/web/src/preview/fixtures.tsx` for the case you're changing.

## HTML artefacts (mockups, visual reports, explainers)

Standalone HTML produced for a human to view — a mockup, a visual report, an
explainer — goes in the gitignored `.artifacts/` directory at the worktree
root: write it with the ordinary file-write tool and cite the
workspace-relative path (e.g. `.artifacts/quota-mockup.html`) in chat, which
renders it in-app via the file chip's View affordance. Relative subresources
resolve, so a multi-file artefact works — keep all its files under one
subdirectory of `.artifacts/`. Pick a fresh descriptive filename and never
overwrite an existing artefact — the worktree may be shared with other
threads, and a chat chip renders whatever is on disk now. Do not write
renderable HTML to locations outside the worktree (the `visual_explainer`
tool's `~/.agent/diagrams/` default cannot be rendered in-app — write the
HTML to `.artifacts/` instead), and do not commit throwaway HTML under
`experiments/` or `docs/`. For a reviewable plan or recap, prefer the MDX
genres (`plans/<slug>/plan.mdx`, `recaps/<slug>/recap.mdx`) over a standalone
HTML artefact.

## Fork-specific notes

- Loom is a **Pi-first fork**: `PI_DEFAULT_MODEL` is the default model and the
  driver registry deliberately ships pi only. Upstream's multi-provider
  guidance ("Providers: Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, and OpenCode each have an
  adapter") applies to the adapters that remain, not to the registry.
- Upstream sync doctrine and per-area resolutions live in
  [`docs/upstream-sync/`](docs/upstream-sync/).
- **Mark every loom hunk.** Any hunk you add to a file that also exists
  upstream carries a `// loom:` comment; larger additions belong in a
  `*.loom.ts` module or `apps/web/src/loom/`. Unmarked hunks are invisible to
  the lost-feature audit and are silently dropped at the next upstream pull.
  The `pnpm ship` gate enforces this
  (`docs/upstream-sync/pull7-tools/unmarkedsweep.sh`); the convention is in
  [`docs/upstream-sync/23-sidebar-v2-rehome.md`](docs/upstream-sync/23-sidebar-v2-rehome.md).
- **Never `git stash` in this repo.** Every worktree shares one `.git`, so the
  stash stack is global across all concurrent threads and a `pop` can hand you
  another thread's work and drop yours. Commit a WIP (`--no-verify`) or use
  `git diff > patch` / `git apply` instead.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.
2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.
3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.

## Hit every surface

The most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:

- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`
- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is "not supported here".
- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.
- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.
- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.
- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.
- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.

## Dev servers

- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.
- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins. The server enforces the same default: a checkout provisioned under `<home>/worktrees/` runs on its own `.t3` even when booted by hand as `node apps/server/src/bin.ts serve`, and one INFO line at startup names the rule that chose the home. Passing `--base-dir "$PWD/.t3"` still says it explicitly, and remains the habit worth keeping. A boot also refuses outright when another live server already holds that home's database (`statev2.sqlite`); clear it by deleting `<stateDir>/server-runtime.json` only when you know that pid is not a server.
- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.
- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. It carries standard scopes, while the startup URL carries admin scopes needed for Connections settings.
- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).
- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.

## Test data

An empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:

- Run `vp run migrate-dev-db` with your dev server stopped. It rebuilds `<worktree>/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` from a read-only snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite`, the developer's real data. It keeps recent projects and their stopped threads, and drops scheduled tasks, pending work, and auth sessions, so your dev server never runs the developer's agents. Raise `--projects` and `--threads-per-project` for more data.
- Refresh `statev2.sqlite`, not `state.sqlite`. The server copies the V1 `state.sqlite` only when `statev2.sqlite` is missing.
- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.
- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works. `vp test run <files>` for the tests you touched, targeted lint and typecheck for the scope you changed.
- Test meaningful logic or observable behavior. Do not render components to static markup to assert props or attributes, or add tests that merely assert callback wiring or mirror the implementation.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong.
- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.

For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is a build step, not a blocker. Run `node scripts/mobile-native-client.ts ensure <ios|android> <device-id>` on the simulator host before starting Metro. It checks the local Expo fingerprint and builds/installs when needed. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.

## Pull requests

- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.
- When babysitting: poll checks and comments newer than the last push, verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.

## Documentation

Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.

- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
- Keep a local implementation explanation in a nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.

## Plans and work artifacts

- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.

## How it works

Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.

Architecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`

## Where code lives

- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency.

## Taste

- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations. See [Web UI](docs/internals/web-ui.md).
- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
- Comments describe how a thing is used, and move when the code moves. To be used mostly to describe functions, not to annotate every line of behavior.
- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.

## Additional tips

- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

An implementation agent is consulting you about a decision it cannot resolve from the implementation plan and the codebase alone.
Use ONLY the inherited snapshot conversation (and read-only file inspection if absolutely needed) to answer.
Return the structured answer shape exactly as defined in your system prompt. Do not add preamble.

## Author lane
You were named explicitly. Answer from your own context only; defer questions outside your scope.

## Observation
The plan/brief rule 'migration 1052 only; 1051 stays free' collides with an existing invariant test: apps/server/src/persistence/LoomMigrations.test.ts asserts the Loom ledger is DENSE 1001..CURRENT_LOOM_LANE_END (13 tests fail with 1052 registered after 1050). The density rule exists because Migrator runs only ids above the high-water mark: once any database has run 1052, a later migration numbered 1051 can never run there — so a 'free' 1051 is in fact permanently unusable, not reserved. Nothing in the tree or the plan uses 1051 (the search-option reservation was dropped in DL-500).

## Decision being considered
Number the import-ledger migration 1051 (dense lane, test untouched) or keep 1052 and teach LoomMigrations.test.ts to expect a permanent hole at 1051?

## Options
1. A: number it 1051_LoomLegacyImports (lane stays dense; record the departure from the brief in a DL row)
2. B: keep 1052 and amend the density test to allow a documented hole at 1051 (1051 is then unusable forever)
3. Escalate to the user

## Worker's recommendation
A — the only reason for 1052 was a since-dropped reservation; a hole buys nothing and weakens a guard that exists to catch exactly this class of mistake.

## Blast radius if the recommendation is wrong
Migration ids are permanent once a database runs them; the QA world is built from this branch next, so the number must be settled before the QA build. Docs (plan, verify.sql H 'MAX(migration_id) = 1052', QA guide) would need 1052 → 1051.

## Worker-supplied evidence
- apps/server/src/persistence/LoomMigrations.test.ts:249 'both lanes end dense and correct' asserts ledgerIds(loom) == range(1001, CURRENT_LOOM_LANE_END)
- apps/server/src/persistence/LoomMigrations.ts header: 'Migrator.make decides what to run with a high-water mark ... if (currentId <= latestMigrationId) continue'
- plan recorded fact 2: '1051 is free and stays free — Phase 4 uses 1052 only'

content.text:
## Answer
Take option A: number the import ledger `1051_LoomLegacyImports` and keep the lane dense. The snapshot's only reason for 1052 was a reservation of 1051 that has since been dropped; "1051 stays free" was never load-bearing and, given the high-water-mark rule, cannot be honoured anyway.

## Confidence
medium

## Evidence
- The Phase 4 plan review (nice-to-have 4) said the 1052 note was stale because "the revised Phase 3 assigns 1051 to attentionEpisodes (3b, conditional), and search is deferred" — the only justification for skipping 1051 was a Phase 3 reservation that did not materialise (the migrations directory ends at `1050_LoomThreadReroute.ts`).
- Phase 3's record (doc 31 §2) framed 1051 as "free for a track that discovers a table; 1052 is Phase 4's" — a sequencing convenience between parallel tracks, not a constraint with a reason behind it.
- The orchestrator's fold (recorded fact 2 / DL-500) rewrote the note to "1051 is free and stays free — Phase 4 uses 1052 only" while unaware of the density invariant in `LoomMigrations.test.ts`; the brief's "leave it" carried the parent orchestrator's instruction verbatim, again with no stated reason.
- No QA world has been built yet from this branch (the QA-build node is unbriefed, blocked on the importer gate), so no persistent database has run a Loom migration above 1050.

## Reasoning
The snapshot said: 1052 was chosen because 1051 was thought reserved; that reservation was later dropped; the number was kept out of inertia ("the number is still right"), not because anything depended on the gap. The snapshot did not know the Loom ledger has a density test, nor that `Migrator` skips ids below the high-water mark — the worker's observation is new and shows "free" was a fiction. Inferring from that: option B would weaken a guard that exists to catch exactly this mistake in order to preserve a number nobody needs, which is the opposite of the plan's stated discipline (migrations in the Loom lane only, upstream's ledger untouched, nothing silently disabled). Option A is the implementation-level correction and costs only doc and `verify.sql` edits before any database exists.

## Scope of impact
implementation only

## Recommended action for the worker
Proceed with option A: create `1051_LoomLegacyImports.ts`, register it in `LoomMigrations.ts`, leave the density test as is; update the `1052` references you can reach on your branch (`scripts/pull9-qa/verify.sql` H `MAX(migration_id) = 1051`, the plan's file-tree note and recorded fact 2, doc 32 §2 "Phase 4 uses 1052 only"); record the departure as a DL row in your range (DL-510+) naming the density invariant as the reason, and state the change prominently in your report so the QA-build brief and Carl's guide say 1051.

## When to escalate to the user instead
If any persistent database that will continue to be used (not a throwaway smoke home) has already run a Loom migration numbered ≥ 1051 — e.g. a QA world or dev home built from a branch where 1052 existed — because then re-numbering would skip the ledger on that database; otherwise this needs no human decision.
